reasoning: All six failure edits are kept first and unchanged in substance, since they fix observed failures: time-relative clues, bare proper names for mint/river/university, single-name rulers, fragment and title clues, parenthetical hints, and the singular/plural number rule. I made one small edit to the first failure edit. Its Hussein example now says to answer 'King Hussein', so it agrees with the ruler carve-out. Seven of the eight success edits are kept because they cover patterns the failure edits do not: definition/etymology clues, meaning/translation and letter framing, epithet/attribution, truncated archive hits, possessive/relational clues, numeric options, alternate-name and description-only clues, and 'group of X' plurals. Three failure/success pairs targeted the same anchor line, so I moved the success edits to distinct anchors to avoid ordering ambiguity. The Honor-qualifiers anchor stays with the failure edit. The alternate-name and description-only edit now anchors after the Rule 1 double-meaning bullet. The meaning/translation and letter-framing edit now anchors after the bare date + place bullet, one line before the Jokes anchor that the failure edit keeps. The 'group of X' plural rule is compatible with the failure number rule, because 'Hamstrings' is a normally plural noun. No edits touch the protected SLOW_UPDATE section.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content:
- Time-relative words in the clue ('current', 'present', 'now', 'today', 'new', 'latest') are frozen at the date the clue was written. Do NOT answer with today's holder of the office. Anchor on the distinctive biographical or factual details (schools, birthplace, deeds) and choose the person the passages tie to them, even if that person is no longer 'current'. Example: 'This current king of Jordan ... educated at Harrow & Sandhurst' -> the passage 'Hussein I, king of Jordan; educated in England at Harrow and Sandhurst' wins over the present-day king (answer 'King Hussein', see the single-name ruler rule in Rule 4). A near-verbatim passage match on the clue's details beats the 'current' wording.
- When several near-synonyms fit (hydropower / hydroelectric power / water power), pick the one the passages use in a sentence that echoes the clue's own wording ('the nation's largest renewable electricity source' -> 'Hydroelectric power is the largest source of renewable electricity'). Prefer the one that forms the standard compound with the clue's noun ('type of plant for this' -> 'hydroelectric plant'). When the clue says '<noun> for this' or '<noun> of this', the answer is often the modifier word that precedes that noun, in its adjective form ('hydroelectric').

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - Places and institutions: when the clue says 'this mint / port / river / lake / mountain / airport / college / university / bank / prison / bridge / island / county', the answer key almost always uses the bare proper name. 'whose mark is a "D"' + 'this mint' -> 'Denver' (not 'Denver Mint'); 'this river' -> 'Nile'; 'this university' -> 'Yale'. Strike the type word the clue already gives (mint, river, college) even if the passages write 'Denver Mint'. Keep a head noun only when the bare word names a different thing or is not a complete name ('Roman Empire', 'Gadsden Purchase', 'pituitary gland').

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Rulers known by only a given name: when the answer is a monarch, pope or similar whom the passages call by a single given name (no surname) and the clue says 'this king/queen/pope', keep the title with the name ('King Hussein', 'Queen Victoria'), because the bare given name is ambiguous across dynasties. If a full name or surname exists ('Winston Churchill'), give it without the title.

edits.target: and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Bare place/title fragments: a clue that is only two or more places from one country ('In Dijon & Bordeaux') asks for the shared nationality, language or country adjective ('French'). Do this even when every passage is about trains, hotels, routes or flights: those passages are just search hits for the place names, not hints about the answer, so never answer with a topic word from them ('TGV'). A clue of the form '<Title> <Person name>' ('President Tran Duc Luong', 'Prime Minister X', 'King Y') asks for the country or organization he led ('Vietnam'). Do not answer with the title, 'President of Vietnam', or his name.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - Parenthetical hints that give a role and dates ('(U.S. president, '81-'89)', '(French, 1840-1926)') are not jokes. They define WHO or WHAT the answer is, so resolve them to the named person or thing ('Ronald Reagan') and answer that. Quiz-archive pages list neighbouring clues of the same category together (e.g. a 'Starr witnesses' clue next to the target clue). Never take the answer or key word from an adjacent clue; answer the clue that matches the full wording. For a person the passages call 'Sir X Y', answer 'Sir X Y' or the bare surname ('Drake'); the in-between form 'X Y' ('Francis Drake') usually fails to match.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content:
- Number: use the headword an answer key would use. For a countable thing give the singular even when the clue says 'these' ('these destructive sea waves' -> 'tsunami', not 'tsunamis'; 'Well', not 'wells'). Keep the plural only for nouns that are plural-only or normally plural, and for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Giblets', 'Bananas', 'Scissors').
- 'this/these <thing>' inside a descriptive clue ('pass the gravy made with these turkey innards'): the answer is only the thing described ('Giblets'). Never fuse it with the noun the clue already names ('giblet gravy').
- Definition or synonym clues ('A double that visually resembles another'): the answer is a DIFFERENT word or phrase that means the same ('look-alike'). Never echo the clue's own head noun ('Double'). Look in the passages for thesaurus or dictionary lines such as 'someone closely resembling another' and take the synonym they give.

edits.target: ## Rule 1: Questions are Jeopardy-style clues; always answer with the missing entity
edits.content: - Definition / etymology / jargon clues ('From the Middle Dutch for "little barrel", it's another way of saying yokel', '3 points on one throw in horseshoes', 'term for ...'): the answer is the defined WORD or technical term itself. Look for the headword of dictionary-style passages (the entry whose etymology or synonym list matches the clue) or the scoring or jargon term in the rules passages ('ringer'). Answer with that bare term. Never answer with a synonym already named in the clue (yokel, hayseed) or with a descriptive phrase.

edits.target: Give the bare name ('Ronald Reagan'), not the event, the place or the date.
edits.content:
- Meaning/translation clues ('The name of these Russian spacecraft means "union"', 'Latin for ...'): the clue gives the English meaning and the answer is the original-language name or word. Find the passage that glosses it ('Russian Soyuz, literally union') and answer with that name (Soyuz). Do not answer with the English meaning or with a related program or agency.
- Letter, postcard or message framing ('Dear Gary, ... Today we visited this "Happiest Place on Earth" -- wish you were here!') is decoration. Use the quoted epithet, slogan or nickname plus any place or date as the anchor, and answer with the entity that epithet names ('Disneyland'). If the matching archive line is truncated before the answer, confirm it from other passages that pair the epithet with that entity.

edits.target: When passages are noisy, use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
edits.content:
- Alternate-name clues ('...as the U.S. holiday Decoration Day', 'formerly known as X', 'also called X'): the clue already gives ONE name for the thing, so the answer is the OTHER name. Look for passages saying 'originally/formerly called X' or 'X, now Y' and answer with Y ('Memorial Day'), never the name already in the clue.
- Description-only clues (a formula, procedure, property or definition, e.g. 'To get this quadrilateral's area, add the 2 parallel sides, divide by 2 & multiply by the height'): the answer is the named concept that the description defines ('trapezoid'). Take its type from the clue's category noun ('quadrilateral' -> a shape). The passages may only describe it, so use your own knowledge to name it, and prefer the candidate that every detail of the description fits.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Epithet or attribution clues ('X has called him "King of the Techno-Thriller"', 'dubbed "the Iron Lady"'): search the passages for the quoted phrase. The name that sits next to it in many independent passages is the answer, even when the source (a magazine, a critic) is named in the clue. Answer with the person's standard full name, not the critic, the publication or a character.

edits.target: - Archive snippets are often truncated right after the clue (e.g. '...THIS PLAYWRIGHT, DAVID...'). Treat the visible part as a strong hint and complete the answer from other passages repeating the same fact. Choose the entity that recurs across many passages together with the clue's other named entities (e.g. the title in 'Thunder Road (film)' pages). Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - If the archive hit is cut off before the answer (e.g. a flashcard dump showing only the clue), do not give up and do not answer 'unknown'. Resolve it from the clue's concrete details (year, distance, landmark, superlative), the supporting passages (including passage titles and headwords that repeat the same entity), and your own knowledge. Choose the one entity that fits every detail ('175 miles north of Calgary' + 1947 oil -> Edmonton). Do not switch to a related item such as a theme song, a subordinate character or a Roman counterpart.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Possessive and relational clues ('his grandfather, the adding machine inventor, ...'; 'this woman's NYC gallery') ask for the owner or descendant the pronoun points to, not the relative, object or institution already described in the clue. Give that person's full name as the passages repeat it ('William S. Burroughs', 'Peggy Guggenheim').

edits.target: - Clue lists its own options ('Of North Park, East Park, West Park or South Park, it's where...'): the answer is exactly one of the listed options, copied verbatim. Use the context to pick which.
edits.content: - Numeric options ('Of 2, 5 or 10, the number of eyes on a bee'): the passages may give only parts (2 compound eyes, 3 simple eyes) or a headline figure for a sub-type. Add up the components and prefer a passage that states the total ('a bee has 5 eyes'). Then answer with the listed number that matches the overall total, not the first number you meet. Give just the digit or number.

edits.target: ## Rule 4: Exact-match formatting of the final answer
edits.content: - 'This group of <category noun>' ('this group of muscles at the back of the thigh') asks for the group's standard name in its customary form, usually plural ('Hamstrings'), without the category noun ('muscles').
